Once a country makes that major scientific jump, adding on a robot arm to attack or an additional system to jam is just a matter of time and energy.
Another reason RPOs may be favored would be to avoid the debris problem caused by using kinetic anti-satellite weapons, such as missiles.
The US has said it is hoping to make major advancements in stationing anti-missile physical interceptors in space that can protect satellites by 2028.
Despite all this focus on RPOs for the US, China, and Russia, Israel has expressed keen interest regarding space weapons in relation to lasers.
On June 29, Defense Minister Israel Katz told a briefing of military reporters that Israel is developing space lasers to carry out attacks above the Earth.
This was an expansion and more specific version of a statement which Katz made earlier in June, when he committed Israel to becoming the leading player with space attack capabilities.
“One of the central goals which the prime minister and I set is that we are recruiting the best minds,” since “as of today, no country has the ability to mount attacks in space. We must be the leading country in the world with this capability,” said Katz.
The defense minister continued, “If we achieve this, it will ensure the advantage of deterrence, of the ability to attack, destroy, and all of the other matters, versus our enemies with large resources.”
Lasers to be used to defend Israeli assets
But Monday was the first time that Katz specifically mentioned space lasers.
Israel is already a leading country in developing Iron Beam as a land-based space laser, and during a visit to Elbit earlier in the summer, The Jerusalem Post saw and heard about work on presumed future fighter-jet-based lasers.
Overall, it seemed clear that Katz on June 29 was referring to Iran.
This is especially true since during the 2026 war, Israel struck multiple Iranian space war-related facilities, including facilities working on developing capabilities to attack satellites in space.
It was unclear if he indirectly also wanted to deter Russia and China from assisting Iran in this and other spheres.
According to foreign reports, lasers might be able to destroy enemy satellites and also burn up any debris that an attack in space by other means might cause.
Some have already speculated that Israel could destroy enemy space satellites using the Arrow 3 missile system, given that it already strikes ballistic missiles in space.
Yet, due to the same issue that Russia and China already fell into regarding debris, many countries are working on other techniques, such as paralyzing, damaging, jamming, dragging, or using lasers against satellites in space.
While some Israeli officials have hinted at such efforts, Katz’s public statements on June 29 were the clearest one to date by a senior Israeli official.
Why the US's first focus is on RPOs
In contrast, if Iran or other enemies advanced past Israel in space, they could attack Israeli satellites and reduce its surveillance capabilities.
After all of this, why then do most experts believe that the US's first and current focus is on RPOs, and not lasers?
It is not that the US and the other countries with space programs are not working on developing space lasers. They are.
Also, Israel’s success with developing the Iron Beam for actual deployments as a ground laser has spurred other countries forward in the more general laser defense area.
But lasers in space or on aircraft are still a distant solution, as they involve a series of more complex physics and engineering problems, which invariably will take longer to solve than RPOs.
RPOs are thereby an immediate answer to help deter enemies from attacking, since they can be used to attack enemy satellites, as well as providing defense against other countries’ potential RPO attacks.
If enemies have existing and immediate weapons to attack an object, such as a satellite, the US and other countries, potentially even including Israel, are likely to focus on immediate solutions, with the focus on space lasers being a longer-term goal.
In that sense, the US statement in September was about immediately deterring China and Russia from attacking American satellites.
In contrast, Katz’s June statement was less about immediate attack, defense, or deterrence.
Rather, it was more about either bragging to the Israeli public about a future distant achievement, or psychological warfare against Iran to the extent that the Islamic Republic might believe it can work with Moscow and Beijing to go after Israel’s satellite advantage.

articles.title: 1,125 Kyiv residents injured in Russian attacks since the start of 2026, more than a third of them in five weeks from late August, Kyiv health chief says
articles.body:
Russian attacks have injured 1,125 Kyiv residents since the start of 2026. Of these, 379 people, or nearly 34%, were injured in just five weeks, from 27 August to 7 October, Tetiana Mostepan, director of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health, said in an interview published on 13 October.
Russian air attacks on Kyiv have intensified since late August. Air attacks occur both day and night, and Russian drones target not only military facilities but also civilian buildings, including apartments. As a result, the number of casualties is also increasing. More than 40% of emergency medical responses to attacks this year occurred between late August and early October, Mostepan noted.
During this period, the capital’s emergency medical teams responded to 782 calls related to the attacks, the department director said. She also released data showing that 138 medical facilities in Kyiv have been damaged since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, including 47 this year.
“And when we talk about statistics, I always emphasize that behind every number is a human life. These are people who have been injured, as well as medical workers who respond to attack sites to save them,” Mostepan said.
Russian attacks on Kyiv have become more frequent
Russia attacked Kyiv with drones throughout the day, Suspilne Kyiv reported on 27 August. Air raid alerts were issued 12 times in the capital, drone debris was found in five districts, and at least four people were injured, the report said. Russian forces used about 140 attack drones against Ukraine throughout the day, more than 100 of them jet-powered, the Ukrainian Air Force reported at the time.
At least 38 people were killed and dozens injured in a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot in the Bucha district near Kyiv, triggering a massive fire and hours of explosions in a residential area, CNN reported. The attack in the Bucha district came amid near-constant Russian airstrikes, which continued into Sunday, the outlet reported.
Russian forces were likely seeking to exhaust Ukraine’s air defenses, disrupt civilians’ daily lives, and increase the scale of destruction, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, citing CNN’s reporting.
On 8 September, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stressed the urgent need to strengthen support for Ukraine, particularly by providing air defense systems. Delays in delivering assistance cost human lives, he said.
On 1 October, a Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while 104 children were inside, Suspilne reported. Students and school staff took shelter, so no one was injured, the report said.
Russian attacks continue after Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire
Following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, Russia continued striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, including in Kyiv. On 13 October, Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv, hitting a thermal power plant in the second attack in 24 hours without advance warning from Ukraine’s allies, Zelenskyy said. The evening and morning strikes killed four people in Kyiv, three of them women in a high-rise in Desnianskyi district, Kyiv prosecutors said.
Russia attacked energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv with 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 14 October. At least 600,000 people were left without electricity, he said. Later that day, an accident on the grid cut power to part of Kyiv’s right bank, energy company DTEK said.
Read also
- Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
- US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms

articles.title: Former Ukrainian president Yushchenko writes open letter to Trump
articles.body:
Former Ukrainian president Yushchenko writes open letter to Trump
Viktor Yushchenko, Ukraine's third president, has written an open letter to US President Donald Trump over his agreement with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin on diesel fuel.
Source: Yushchenko on Facebook
Quote: "And against this reality, Ukrainians hear calls that Ukraine should stop. That Ukraine should restrain its strikes against the infrastructure that finances and sustains Russia's war. That trade in Russian energy can somehow be separated from the missiles and drones Russia sends against Ukrainian families. It cannot.
Money paid for Russian fuel is not an abstraction called 'commerce' It finances an economy geared toward total war."
Details: Yushchenko also reflected on events more than three decades ago, when the Soviet Union was breaking up.
He noted that Ukraine had then possessed the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal. "In negotiations with our allies, we agreed to give it up. We did so because we believed that a world governed by agreements was safer than a world governed by nuclear weapons."
Quote: "In 1994, the United States of America, along with its partners, signed the Budapest Memorandum, providing Ukraine with official assurances of security, sovereignty, and the inviolability of our borders.
They pledged not to threaten or use force against Ukraine. America assumed a moral responsibility toward Ukraine. So how can anyone today, when a treacherous enemy has attacked us, forget America's signature on this document?"
Background:
- On 9 October, Trump said he had spoken to Putin and reached an agreement with him on the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's decision to unilaterally lift sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel fuel was unfair and dishonest.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine leave 600,000 without power as Zelenskyy says Moscow ‘disrespecting’ US – Europe live
articles.body:
No indication intelligence sharing with Ukraine has stopped, EU says
The European Commission declined to comment on reported disruption to Starlink’s services in Ukraine, but said there are “no indication that [US] intelligence sharing has stopped.”
Repeatedly asked about the issue, the commission spokespeople said they were “aware of the report” on Starlink, but declined to comment “until we have more information.”
“[It is] important also to say that we have no indications that, intelligence sharing has stopped,” the chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, said.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
The European Commission and Nato’s Mark Rutte have said there were no sign that US intelligence sharing with Ukraine stopped, despite growing concerns after Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night (11:45, 12:44).
But it declined to comment on concerns about apparent restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals, which are critical for its military operations.
Zelenskyy is in Britain this afternoon, with talks with UK prime minister Andy Burnham this afternoon (15:01, 15:28), before going to Brussels to meet EU leaders later this week (16:29).
In other news,
Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz warned German lawmakers about “the time of upheaval,” as he assured of his support for Ukraine and spoke of his government’s priorities in the face of surging support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (14:31).
A Ukrainian soldier led a team of divers that laid explosives on the bed of the Baltic Sea to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines, possibly on the order of state authorities, a court has heard as the much-awaited trial related to the incident got under way in Hamburg (10:43, 14:16).
Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte urged allies to “do more” in the face of “Russia’s aggression unrelenting,” as he insisted the alliance had “all the response options we need” to react to any Russian threat (11:42, 11:45)
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Zelenskyy to attend European Council in Brussels, hold first talks with Hungary's Magyar
Back to Ukraine,Zelenskyy’s schedule for the coming days appears to be getting a bit clearer.
As reported earlier, he is in London today and meeting with UK’s Andy Burnham before joining EU leaders in Brussels later this week for talks on the margins of the European Council.
And Hungary’s Péter Magyar has just said he will also hold his first one-on-one talks with Zelenskyy on Friday, just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest’s longstanding concerns over minority rights.
The move and the talks could unblock Ukraine’s EU accession talks after lengthy hold-ups under the previous Hungarian government of Viktor Orbán.
Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.
Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.
He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.
The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.
It is mainly aimed at China, which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.
“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.
“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.
Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.
French minister accuses Elon Musk of ‘online harassment campaigns’ against European leaders
Ashifa Kassam
European community affairs correspondent
Meanwhile, France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election.
Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy.
“The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said.
The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said.
“They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.”
Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls.
“The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.”
Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
Peter Walker
Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.
The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”
To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.
In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.
Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader, and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.
Burnham pledges to try to 'repair bridges' between Zelenskyy and Trump
UK prime minister Andy Burnham said he will seek to “repair bridges” between US president Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy amid strained ties between the pair, AFP reported.
Burnham made the comments before he was due to welcome Zelensky to his official Downing Street residence, in a show of support for Ukraine’s president after new criticism by Trump.
“What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back,” Burnham told the British parliament.
“Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together. That is the role I intend to play.”
The pair is expected to meet this afternoon, and the Ukrainian president is also expected to meet King Charles III.
Interestingly, Zelenskyy departed for London from the Polish city in Rzeszów reverting to flying from Poland after months of flying from Moldova’s Chișinău during a period of strained relations with Poland over history.
Merz calls for 'creative efforts' to tame the rise of extremism
In pretty pointed remarks against the surging far-right Alternative fur Deutschland, Merz also recalls the opening line from the 1950 Schuman declaration, which said:
“World peace cannot be safeguarded without the making of creative efforts proportionate to the dangers which threaten it.”
Adapting it to today’s Germany and Europe, Merz urges parties to recommit to that “creative effort” and not “a scornful desire for disintegration, a delight in division, or exclusion or fear of others.”
“We must summon that effort and we will - not least in the face of the extremism that has always been a part of our society and is now surging with full force into this parliament, into state parliaments, and into the everyday life of our country.”
He acknowledges that “this extremism … has roots in legitimate dissatisfaction and legitimate feelings of injustices,” but insists it would not resolve any of the people’s problems.
Merz warns of 'time of upheaval' as he doubles down on support for Ukraine and proposes new trade measures to protect EU industries
Over in Berlin, Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is addressing the Bundestag, talking about his government’s plan of reforms, his plans for this week’s EU summit in Brussels and Ukraine.
He warns lawmakers that Germany faces “a time of upheaval, with crises and wars, some of which lie beyond our control.”
Merz repeats his key lines on the much-needed investment in Germany’s defence capabilities, and doubles down on his support for Ukraine.
He dismisses any suggestion that Germany’s support for Ukraine comes at an expense of social and welfare spending.
“This is simply not a case. Not a single euro flowing to Ukraine is being diverted from social or educational spending in our own country. Not a single euro,” he said.
Merz warns that “the danger is very real and concrete,” as Russia continues to show “willigness to escalate: against Ukraine, against our eastern European neighbours, and indeed against our own country.”
“Against this backdrop … it is incomprehensible to me how those on the far left and far right continue to play down the situation,” he said.
He says some comments were almost “deliberately driving the division … and disinformation” to “derivse partisan, political advantages from it.”
Turning to this week’s EU summit, Merz says the discussions will focus on the next EU budget with “negotiations now entering a decisive phase.”
He stresses Germany’s priorities of security and competitiveness, with a call to “further cut back EU bureaucracy and accelerate approval processes to boost and enable investment across Europe,” particularly in decarbonisation, AI and defence.
He also talks about the importance of a new legal regime for pan-European startups, advancing the EU’s capital markets union, and on developing new trade relationships with global partners while reducing “one-sided dependencies” with existing partners.
“We will no longer stand idly by while other states harm our economy through heavy subsidies, artificially devalued currencies, overcapacity, and aggressive pricing. We will not stand idly by any longer.”
(Yep, he probably means China.)
His comments come ahead of his planned trips to Japan, South Korea and Singapore.
He says the European Council will discuss creating “a new trade defence instrument” to respond “swiftly and forcefully to targeted attacks on our industries and supply chains.”
“These decisions would, among other things, provide the European Commission with a tool to react rapidly without needing to consult the European Council first. The European Council, for its part, would then have the power to reverse such a move by a qualified majority. This makes us faster and more effective, and gives the Commission a powerful tool.”
Nord Stream suspect's lawyers argue Nord Stream may have not been a crime, ask for case to be dismissed
Over in Germany, we have an update on the Nord Stream trial which began in Hamburg earlier today (10:43).
Defence lawyers for a former Ukrainian army officer charged with damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines in blasts four years ago have called for the dismissal of charges in the first day of his trial.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Serhii Kuznetsov’s lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany’s imports of natural gas before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a “Russian weapon” and therefore potentially a legitimate target, Reuters reported.
“Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor’s infrastructure without harming any human beings?”
Kuznietsov’s lawyers also argued that he was still an active duty solider an as such was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak about anything during his service for reasons of secrecy linked to national security, AP reported.
Protesters gathered outside the Hamburg court in support of the defendant, with a sign that read: “What are war crimes?”
“Russia is the only war criminal that belongs in the dock,” said one of the dozens of protesters.
Bulgaria says Russia likely behind Black Sea drone strikes but 'we cannot prove it'
In the Bulgarian parliament, prime minister Rumen Radev has said that Russia was most likely behind drone attacks in the Black Sea that sank two ships, but that “we cannot prove it”.
AP quotes Radev saying “There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favours Russia, and indeed, the logic points in that direction. The problem is that we cannot prove it.”
The Russian ambassador to Bulgaria was summoned yesterday over the issue, and Bulgarian president Iliana Yotova has called for an immediate halt to hostilities in the Black Sea and a moratorium on drone attacks against commercial and civilian infrastructure.
Bulgaria investigating report that Starlink antennas set on fire near Sofia
Bulgaria is investigating a report that several antennas used for communication with the Starlink satellite network were deliberately set on fire, prime minister Rumen Radev has said.
“The investigation is extremely intensive. We are working with partner services to successfully carry out this operation,” AFP reports Radev said in parliament, without confirming or denying the claim.
A Bulgarian opposition MP has claimed 11 telecommunications antennas linked to the Starlink network were set on fire over the weekend “at a secret facility near Sofia”.
A spokesperson for the Sofia prosecutor’s office confirmed to AFP that an investigation was under way but said no one has been charged.
A fire broke out at a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in September, with the country’s digital affairs minister calling the blaze an act of “sabotage” and prime minister Donald Tusk describing it as an “act of hybrid warfare”.
Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, has said his country has not observed a substantial reduction in US support for Ukraine, and does not expect to. The statement comes amid the US and Russia having secured a diesel supply deal, and reports that Elon Musk’s Starlink service has been reduced for Ukrainian forces.
Moscow has said that the US-Russia deal over diesel “will open other opportunities as well”.
Reuters reports Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Moscow would overcome any sanctions-related difficulties to ensure the diesel supplies were delivered, and that the deal could pave the way for further economic cooperation between the two nations.
Reuters, citing local media, reports that Bulgaria expects to join a Nato anti-drone initiative by the end of October. The news comes a day after a drone attack sank a cargo vessel off the country’s Black Sea coast for the second time in a week.
Defence minister Dimitar Stoyanov said “Bulgaria will be part of this project as soon as possible. Expectations are that by 30 October, we will already be part of the project.”
Eutelsat shares jump as Ukraine flags curbs on Starlink military-grade service
And Reuters is reporting that shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat rose sharply on Wednesday after Ukraine said SpaceX’s Starlink had introduced restrictions on its military-grade service, fuelling investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
Eutelsat shares were up 11.6% by late morning, while Luxembourg-based rival SES, which also provides satellite connectivity services, gained 2.7%.
No indication intelligence sharing with Ukraine has stopped, EU says
The European Commission declined to comment on reported disruption to Starlink’s services in Ukraine, but said there are “no indication that [US] intelligence sharing has stopped.”
Repeatedly asked about the issue, the commission spokespeople said they were “aware of the report” on Starlink, but declined to comment “until we have more information.”
“[It is] important also to say that we have no indications that, intelligence sharing has stopped,” the chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, said.
EU 'headed for a very, very difficult winter,' commission warns as energy markets remain 'very volatile'
The European Commission has warned that the EU is “headed for a very, very difficult winter” with high energy prices expected to cause an affordability crisis and “a very volatile” in the energy markets.
The warning was delivered by the EU’s energy spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen when answering questions about proposed changes adding flexibility to rules on methane imports to help save costs.
She stressed the EU was “not facing a security supply issue for the time being,” but it faced a “very unpredictable” situation in the coming months.
“We do not have visibility, for example, what and when something will happen in the Strait of Hormuz, where 20% of gas and oil is being blocked since many, many months,” she said.
The commission’s chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, added that the changes are needed as “we could not anticipate that we would have a crisis in the Strait of Hormuz,” which continues to affect prices and supply of energy.
Why is the far right on the rise in Europe? - Reddit AMA
Lucy O’Brien
This summer in Germany, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt.Meanwhile, support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe.
There are now radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.
The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year. How might these elections shape the political future of the continent?
Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam, our European correspondents, will be answering your questions live on Reddit r/geopolitics from 4pm CEST.

articles.title: FACTBOX: SpaceX restricts access to Starlink for Ukrainian military
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. SpaceX limited the speed of Starlink satellite internet terminals used by the Ukrainian army overnight, Sergey Beskrestnov, Vladimir Zelensky’s external adviser and expert in communications and unmanned systems, said.
Below are the main facts on the subject.
Restriction of access
- SpaceX imposed restrictions on the operation of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian army overnight, disrupting its operations, Sergey Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, wrote on Telegram.
- Sternenko speculated that SpaceX had acted at the request of US President Donald Trump’s administration.
- Zelensky’s external adviser Beskrestnov later confirmed the reports on Telegram.
- According to him, the restrictions currently apply to the ‘military package’ of Starshield services, with the speed limit set at 100 miles per hour (about 160 kilometers per hour - TASS).
- This "disrupted a number of missions," Beskrestnov said.
- In his view, "this action cannot be a coincidence and has to do with the current political situation."
- Ukraine once again received no intelligence warning from its Western partners last night, Vladimir Zelensky said.
- The US warned Ukraine that it could suspend intelligence sharing, Zelensky said in an interview with NPR. According to him, Ukrainian generals reported that they had been notified of this possibility at the military level.
- Ukraine received no intelligence warnings regarding the first wave of Russian ballistic missile launches overnight into October 14, but warnings about subsequent attacks did come in, RBC Ukraine quoted Ukrainian Air Force Spokesman Yury Ignat as saying.
Consequences
- A slowdown in Starlink service is making it virtually impossible to launch medium-range drones, and some missions involving them have already been cancelled since the start of the day, the 7th Corps of the Ukrainian airborne assault troops reported on Telegram.
- The Ukrainian armed forces rely entirely on Starlink satellite internet, so the Kiev authorities must travel to the US to negotiate the lifting of access restrictions, Verkhovna Rada lawmaker Alexey Goncharenko (listed in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) said.
- The Ukrainian army will no longer be able to counter Russian jet-powered drones due to the reduced speed of the US Starlink satellite Internet service, Zelensky’s external adviser on communications and unmanned systems, Beskrestnov, said.
- As the adviser pointed out, Kiev uses Starlink to counter jet-powered drones, but restrictions on its operation will now prevent the Ukrainian military from doing so.
- Beskrestnov said that through their actions Ukraine’s partners "actually deprive" Kiev of one of the few chances to intercept such drones.
- The slowdown of Starlink terminals caught the Ukrainian military by surprise, occurring entirely without warning, the British newspaper Financial Times (FT) wrote citing sources.
- The report says that Ukrainian drones relying on Starlink terminals are experiencing signal disruptions at speeds above 160 kmph.
- The reduction in intelligence-sharing from the United States, combined with Starlink's operational restrictions, is seriously hampering the Ukrainian military, unmanned aviation expert and CEO of the Center for Integrated Unmanned Solutions Dmitry Kuzyakin told TASS.
- According to him, the Kiev regime’s unchecked actions are irritating both the US president himself and a segment of the American establishment that has heavily invested in Ukraine.
- A number of cyber operations by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) against Russia may be disrupted or delayed due to SpaceX restricting the speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by Ukrainian security agencies, Sergey Trukhachev, a technical and digital security expert, told TASS.
- He also noted that the SpaceX restrictions would directly impact the Ukrainian armed forces as well.
- This would primarily affect Ukrainian operators of high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), the expert added.
Response
- Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned US entrepreneur and SpaceX owner Elon Musk on social media platform X, amid reports that connection speeds for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by the Ukrainian military have been throttled.

articles.title: ‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least six, damages power sites
articles.body:
‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least 9, damages power sites
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine’s partners failed to warn of Russian ballistic missiles attack on Kyiv.
Russian air attacks have killed at least nine people in Ukraine and left hundreds of thousands without power, days after United States President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” in the more-than four year war.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Wednesday that its forces had carried out a “massive” strike against communications and energy infrastructure facilities in Ukraine, the Interfax news agency reported.
In a statement, it said Russian forces hit two plants supplying power and heating in the capital Kyiv, two other plants in the wider region and an electricity substation.
Other targets included a heating and power plant in Ukraine’s second-largest city Kharkiv, along with a thermal power facility which the ministry said supplied the Ukrainian military in the southeast of the Kharkiv region.
Moscow said its forces had also hit a data centre in Kyiv which it said was used to gather intelligence on Russia’s military.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to remain in shelters.
“Energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region have come under a massive ballistic missile strike. There are power disruptions in the capital,” he wrote on Telegram.
DTEK, Ukraine’s largest private energy provider, said the attack had caused emergency power cuts in several urban districts of Kyiv.
A Russian strike on a multistorey building in the capital’s Desnianskyi district killed two people, while another attack in Golosiivsky district killed one, Ukraine’s state emergency service said.
The Ukrainian military also reported that two people were killed and six wounded in Russian attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region. Another person was killed in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region.
In the Volyn region, a Russian attack on Ukraine’s western city of Lutsk killed three people and injured at least 12, governor Roman Romaniuk said on Telegram.
Further Russian missile attacks were reported in the Kharkiv and Zhytomyr regions, while other strikes hit Sumy and Chernihiv.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said a record number of hypersonic missiles were used in the attacks on the capital.
“Over half a million people in Ukraine are without power as a result of these strikes,” she said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine received no warnings from its Western partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on the capital, raising questions about intelligence sharing.
“A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners,” he wrote on Facebook. “This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.”
The president said Ukraine detected the missiles only as they neared Kyiv.
He also accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” Trump announced on Sunday.
“A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” he wrote on X.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect towards the United States.”
A technology adviser to the Ukrainian president said the operation of some Starlink internet terminals appeared to have been restricted overnight, preventing its military-grade version from operating above 160 kilometres per hour, disrupting combat missions.
“Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion,” Sergiy Beskrestnov said, referring to Elon Musk’s company, which owns Starlink.
“Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation.”
Russia also reported Ukrainian drone strikes overnight. The governor of Russia’s Saratov region, Roman Busargin, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo.
Busargin said all infrastructure facilities were operating as usual. Balakovo is home to a data centre of Russia’s top lender Sberbank, a nuclear power plant and a hydropower station, whose dam spans the Volga River, among other facilities.
Sberbank later said its data centre in the Saratov region had been attacked by drones, but that all systems were operating as normal.
Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defence forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying towards the Russian capital overnight. Russian authorities said about 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.
Russia’s military later put the number of downed Ukrainian drones overnight at 902, of which 180 were shot down near the capital, Moscow.

articles.title: 'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
articles.body:
'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
Ukraine's Starlink access has been restricted without warning, severely disrupting "several" military missions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
"I confirm that (Starlink owner) SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion last night. Currently, the restriction applies to the StarShield 'military service package' and limits speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour)," he said in a post on social media.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its mid-strike campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones.
This mid-strike campaign has this year allowed Ukraine to strangle Russian logistics, hampering its ability to fight on the front lines.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that speed limitations had been discovered and the cause was being investigated.
"This complicates drone missions —specifically those involving interceptors and mid-range strike drones — and hampers capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relay," the source added.
A soldier working on mid-range strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
Two other commanders — both from elite drone units working on the eastern and southern front lines — reported issues with Starlink terminals on "middle strike" drones flying at higher speeds over the last 24 hours.
Both likewise requested to remain anonymous, and declined to describe the problems in more detail, so as to not assist the enemy.
In a post on social media, Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps said it was experiencing "throttling" of its Starlink connectivity.
"The consequences are already being felt in the field. Since the start of the day alone, a drone unit operating within the 7th Corps' area of responsibility in the Huliaipole sector has had to cancel a number of missions due to these connectivity issues," the corps said.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," Beskrestnov said.
As reported by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened Ukraine with the withholding of intelligence and other assistance in a bid to protect Russian oil refineries.
Beskrestnov did not provide evidence that the Starlink restriction was connected to U.S. pressure on Ukraine, and the White House has not commented on the issue.
Serhii Sternenko, an activist and former advisor to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, also reported the restriction of access, saying "SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the Trump administration."
The development comes after Ukraine worked with SpaceX earlier this year to deactivate unauthorized Starlink terminals being used by Russian forces. Starlink has played a critical role in Ukrainian military communications throughout the full-scale war.
The threats came after a confusing 48 hours during which U.S. President Donald Trump announced a controversial "deal" with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, followed by repeated demands that Ukraine replace Volodymyr Zelensky as president, followed by Trump announcing a unilateral "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which blindsided both Moscow and Kyiv.
Ukraine has since refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries but Russia has continued its blitz on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, most recently overnight on Oct. 14 when "several" power plants in Kyiv were hit. Trump has refused to accuse Russia of breaking the ceasefire.
The reported Starlink restrictions come as questions have been raised about U.S. intelligence sharing in relation to Russian ballistic missile launches, following two straight nights of attack on Kyiv with little to no warning.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Despite the failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 13.
But later that day, around 10:30 p.m. another wave of ballistic missiles hit Kyiv, again without the usual warning.
At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a hit on a residential building in the Desnianskyi District. Three more waves of ballistic missiles struck Kyiv throughout the night.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat told Ukrainian TV that Ukraine received no warnings from its partners about the first wave, though it did for the following three.
"Ukraine did not attack Russian oil refineries, yet Trump has already begun imposing sanctions on my country. Meanwhile, sanctions against Russia have been eased," Sternenko said.

articles.title: Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid
articles.body:
Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukraine’s energy system overnight into 14 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The barrage came three days after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire, which the Kremlin never confirmed, saying on 12 October only that contacts were continuing.
Ukraine held off strikes on Russian energy for two days after the announcement, Zelenskyy wrote on 13 October. Russia’s barrage opened that evening with a ballistic strike on Kyiv. For the second time in two days, it came without a launch warning from partners.
How the night unfolded
The Air Force described one massive combined strike that began at 18:00 on 13 October. By 09:00 the next day, it had counted 39 missiles on ballistic trajectories and 128 drones, aimed mainly at Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv Oblast. Air defenses downed or suppressed four missiles and 115 drones, but missiles and drones hit 22 locations, the Air Force said.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
The first wave hit Kyiv late on 13 October. Its primary target was CHP-4, a key power plant in the city, and there were hits, Zelenskyy said. Ukrainian systems spotted the missiles only on approach, with no warning from partners. After a call with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Zelenskyy wrote that Ukraine had not been warned for the second time. On 13 October, Trump said the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
A Russian strike also hit a high-rise in Desnianskyi district. Rescuers saved 16 residents, the State Emergency Service reported, and three women were killed there, the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office said. The prosecutor’s office counted 19 injured in the building, including a girl officials described as seven or eight, and five more hurt by shattered windows next door. Across Kyiv, the evening and morning attacks killed four people and injured 25, the prosecutor’s office said, while Suspilne counted 32 injured.
The second wave came early on 14 October and hit several of the capital’s energy facilities, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It killed one person in Holosiivskyi district, he added. Russia attacked all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants and key facilities in Kyiv Oblast that power the capital, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Energy company DTEK reported emergency outages in five Kyiv districts.
Damage and demands
Zelenskyy reported damage to facilities and equipment at 26 elements of the power system and at four oil and gas facilities. At least 600,000 people lost electricity, he said, and outages could grow. He called the strike deliberate and said Russia had never before shown such demonstrative disrespect toward America.
He asked Trump for strong sanctions under the Lindsey Graham sanctions law, which he said was recently passed and signed. He also asked for additional Patriot interceptors.
Read also
- US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
- Hours after Trump declared an energy ceasefire, Russia hit Kharkiv power plant, one of 200-plus strikes on Ukraine’s grid this week, Zelenskyy says

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink terminals
articles.body:
Ukraine accuses Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink terminals
Officials say ability to block Russian drones restricted as Kyiv reels from second night of ballistic missile attacks.
Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite services, disrupting its ability to carry out military operations and leaving Kyiv vulnerable to deadly attacks.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that without warning, services had been limited for terminals travelling over 100mph overnight on Wednesday – effectively limiting Ukraine’s ability to launch drones, which use satellite internet to pilot the craft.
Writing on Telegram, defence technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Ukraine was “deprived of one of the few chances to defend itself from Shahed drones”.
He added that frontline logistics and long-distance missions were also disrupted.
The suggestion that Elon Musk’s company had throttled Starlink services drew the ire of Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv’s behalf.
“Hey Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” wrote Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister. “As your European customers, we are watching you.”
The “big man” jibe refers to a public dispute on social media between Musk, Sikorski and United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio in 2025, when the SpaceX boss told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man” on his X platform.
The clash broke out when Musk, the trillionaire former senior adviser to US President Donald Trump and key midterm election donor for his Republican Party, said that Ukraine’s “entire frontline could collapse” if he switched off Starlink.
He later said, “No matter how much I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink will never turn off its terminals … We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.”
‘Cannot be a coincidence’
The slowdown comes after Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv for the second night in a row, killing at least nine people and damaging electricity and heating infrastructure.
Zelenskyy says Ukraine did not receive its usual warnings from Western allies, without specifying which partners.
Trump said the US has not stopped sharing intelligence.
Beskrestnov warned that the slowdown “cannot be a coincidence” after Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel – despite international sanctions to isolate Moscow.
Speaking to AFP, another Ukrainian official accused Washington of throttling Starlink and helping Russia.
On Saturday, Trump suggested Zelenskyy had not done enough to end the war with Russia, blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.

articles.title: Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s power grid
articles.body:
- Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukrainian energy sites overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said.
- Zelenskyy asked Trump for strong sanctions under the Graham law and more Patriot interceptors after the strike hit infrastructure covered by Trump’s ceasefire.
Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine’s energy and critical infrastructure overnight into Oct. 14, knocking out power to at least 600,000 people days after President Donald Trump announced a halt to strikes on energy facilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said that the attack targeted Kyiv, the surrounding Kyiv region and Kharkiv, and damaged equipment at 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four in the oil and gas sector. He warned that outages could spread further and said there were dead and injured, without giving numbers. Repair crews, power company staff and the State Emergency Service were working to restore supply on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy described the ballistic missile salvo as aimed specifically at the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire Trump announced on Truth Social on Oct. 11, and called the scale of the strike deliberate and demonstrative.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
Moscow never confirmed accepting Trump’s energy ceasefire, and its scope remained disputed after the announcement, with a White House official telling Axios that the proposal initially covered oil refineries, while power plants and electricity grids might follow later. Zelenskyy told Fox News on Oct. 12 that Ukraine had held off on striking Russian energy facilities after the announcement, while Russia kept hitting Ukrainian gas and power sites. Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russia had struck electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times in the week before the announcement.
“Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” said Zelenskyy.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of a Russian strike package for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of the country’s air defenses, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot systems to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for additional packages of Patriot interceptors, saying no country should be left alone against Russia.
He also called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the sanctions law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed on Sept. 18 and which gives the president authority to raise tariffs and restrict Russian energy trade, with key measures due to take effect by Oct. 18.
“We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures,” said Zelenskyy.
The strike followed Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement of a deal to release Russian diesel onto U.S. and world markets, starting with 300,000 tons immediately and 500,000 tons in November, after the Treasury waived diesel sanctions until April 2027. Critics in Congress have said the arrangement gives Moscow additional revenue for the war. The White House had not responded publicly to the overnight strike by Wednesday morning, and Russia’s Defense Ministry had not commented on its targets.

articles.title: Russian Missile Strikes Kill 3 In Kyiv, Knock Out Power As Zelenskyy Says West Gave No Warning
articles.body:
KYIV -- Deadly Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukraine pounded civilian and energy sites across the country, leaving hundreds of thousands without power despite a cease-fire previously announced by US President Donald Trump.
Ukrainian authorities said the strikes on October 14 killed at least three people in Kyiv, two in the country's southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region, and at least six more in the western city of Lutsk. Dozens of others, including children, were injured.
"I never thought I would leave the country," Kyiv resident Lana told RFE/RL after a Russian missile struck a high-rise apartment building where she lives. "But for the sake of my [teenage] daughter...I will leave in the near future."
Other strikes on the Ukrainian capital targeted energy facilities. At least five districts were plunged into emergency power outages after a strike hit one of Kyiv's main power plants, energy company DTEK reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones in overnight attacks on Ukraine, adding at least 600,000 people were left without electricity, warning that such outages might become more widespread.
The attacks came days after Trump's announcement of an energy cease-fire between Russia and Ukraine, which neither country said it had been informed of but which Kyiv largely supported.
"Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X, accusing Russian forces of targeting 26 facilities in the country's power system.
"We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond -- and to respond forcefully," he added.
Separately, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv had once again received no advance warning from its Western partners about the Russian missile and drone launches. He added that Ukrainian forces were able to detect the first wave of attacks only when it was approaching Kyiv.
The issue appears to compound the country’s shortage of air-defense missiles, licenses for which Ukraine has been seeking to obtain from the United States in the hope of establishing its own production. Washington has been sending mixed signals about the potential deal.
Following the latest attacks, the EU’s ambassador to Ukraine, Katarina Mathernova, wrote in a post on X that "missing warning means missing time. Time to wake a child. To get downstairs. To reach a shelter."
"Ukraine needs air defense, interceptors and reliable early warnings. Every minute of warning can give someone a chance to survive," Mathernova added.
Meanwhile, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksander Novak also accused Ukraine of attacking Russia's two oil refineries in Saratov and Ryazan regions on October 14, saying Moscow saw "no indication that the Ukrainian side is moving toward an energy cease-fire."
As Russia has been continuing its relentless bombardment of Ukrainian regions, since the beginning of this year, Kyiv has increasingly responded with a campaign of its own. Its long-range strikes have been targeting Russian military and oil-refinery facilities in an effort to curb revenues for the invasion.
Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn, however, denied Novak's accusation, saying Kyiv had struck a data center and another unnamed target in Russia but no refineries.
Days before, Trump demanded Kyiv "damn well stop" hitting Russian oil refineries amid a global energy shortage -- largely caused by the US war with Iran -- after announcing a deal allowing Russian diesel exports following a conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The move sparked criticism from European allies and from Democrats and Republicans, who warned it could embolden Putin to continue his war against Ukraine.
In a letter to Trump, a bipartisan group of 12 senators urged him to withdraw from the diesel deal with Putin, calling it "a gift to our adversary" and "a betrayal of our Allies."
"Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine," the senators wrote in the letter.
Meanwhile, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko, known for his pro-Western politics during his tenor in 2005-2010, addressed an open letter to Trump criticizing his deal with Putin on diesel fuel.
"When there is talk of 'concessions' or deals with Putin, the Kremlin's answer is more missiles, more drones, and more bloodshed. Ukrainian families pay the price," he wrote. "One does not negotiate with tyrants -- one stops them."

articles.title: “It finances an economy geared toward total war”—Ukraine’s third president on the Russian diesel Washington just cleared
articles.body:
Viktor Yushchenko, Ukraine’s president from 2005 to 2010, has written an open letter to US President Donald Trump and posted it on Facebook on 14 October. Without naming it, the letter takes aim at the green light Washington gave Russian diesel trade five days earlier, after a call between Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Russia banned its diesel exports in July amid a fuel crisis at home, after Ukrainian strikes on refineries had already cut those exports, and last week’s US waiver and the supply deal Trump announced with Moscow would put that fuel back on world markets while Russian strikes still kill Ukrainian civilians.
What Yushchenko says Russian fuel buys
Yushchenko wrote that Russian ballistic missiles, Iranian Shahed drones, and aerial bombs strike homes every day and night in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Dnipro, and Kharkiv. Whenever there is talk of “concessions” or deals with Putin, he wrote, the Kremlin answers with more missiles, more drones, and more bloodshed.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
Yushchenko rejected calls for Ukraine to “restrain its strikes against the infrastructure that finances and sustains Russia’s war.”
“Money paid for Russian fuel is not an abstraction called ‘commerce.’ It finances an economy geared toward total war,” he wrote.
Nuclear arms, Pearl Harbor, and Iwo Jima
Yushchenko wrote that Ukraine inherited “one of the largest nuclear arsenals in the world” and agreed to give it up, trusting the words and signatures of great powers. In his view, by signing the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, America took on a moral responsibility toward Ukraine.
He compared trade in Russian energy to America’s trade with Imperial Japan, which included strategically important materials, before the US entered World War II. Washington hoped for years to avoid a wider war in the Pacific, he wrote, but economic pressure and diplomacy could not prevent catastrophe.
Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities
Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. America knows how dangerous it is to believe that trade can tame an aggressor, Yushchenko wrote, adding: “History taught us that lesson at a terrible price.”
He also named two men he called Ukrainian. One was Sergeant Michael Strank, whose family, Yushchenko wrote, came from Lemkivshchyna. The son of immigrants from Czechoslovakia, Strank took part in the famous raising of the US flag on Iwo Jima, according to the Marine Corps. The other was Oleksandr Silvashko, “a Ukrainian boy from the Cherkasy region,” who, Yushchenko wrote, was the first to embrace US Lieutenant William Robertson when American and Soviet forces met at the Elbe in April 1945.
“One does not negotiate with tyrants—one stops them,” Yushchenko concluded.
Read also
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
- Bipartisan US senators say Trump’s Russian diesel deal conflicts with 2022 ban, as he presses Kyiv to spare Russian refineries
- Deals with dictators lead to hell: Estonia’s PM urges Europe to help Ukraine destroy Russia’s refineries after Washington eased sanctions on diesel

articles.title: Air Force Tests New Sentinel Reentry Vehicle
articles.body:
The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center tested its new intercontinental ballistic missile reentry vehicle Oct. 9, launching the developmental vehicle atop a Minotaur I rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.
The Mk21A reentry vehicle, mated to the Sentinel ICBM, will eventually replace the Minuteman III as the land-based leg of the nation’s nuclear triad. Carrying the new W87-1 nuclear warhead, it will launch atop the Sentinel’s three rocket stages, blasting into space before reentering the atmosphere to strike its target.
The Oct. 9 test launch carried no warhead and was the first announced test of the new vehicle since June 2024.
“The Mk21A is crucial to modernizing our ICBMs in response to the rapidly changing global threat picture posed by our adversaries,” said Maj. Gen. William Rogers, the Air Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for ICBMs, in a statement. “The reentry vehicle’s development will ensure a safe, secure and effective deterrent for generations to come.”
The Mk21A is based on the Mk21 reentry vehicle used on the Minuteman III, and is being developed by Lockheed Martin. The Minotaur I launch vehicle, provided by Northrop Grumman, is based on the Peacekeeper and Minuteman rocket motors. The Space Force helped oversee the test through its Rocket Systems Launch Program, which provides commercial launch systems and excess ballistic missile assets for government payloads.
The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center awarded Lockheed a $996 million contract for the Mk21A in October 2023 and followed with an additional $453 million contract modification in November 2025.
According to an April acquisition report released by the Pentagon in September, the latest contract modification was part of a new baseline for the program intended to “decouple its schedule from external programs and continue development with an updated, more resilient plan.”
The LGM-35 Sentinel program office is still working to overcome the cost and schedule problems that triggered a mandatory Pentagon review, and while officials claim progress, the program is undergoing a restructuring before it can meet Milestone B, which would authorize it to move into engineering and manufacturing development.
The acquisition report offers scant details on the Mk21A rebaseline effort, beyond noting that it includes a new “alternate flight test strategy” and additional test assets. It does note, however, that the June 2024 test successfully flight-tested the vehicle’s heatshield, and that Lockheed was working on integrating the arming and fuzing subsystem in February 2026. Air Force budget documents released in April projected “flight test of heatshield test vehicle and W87-1 environmental flight test unit” in fiscal 2026 and 2027.
A critical design review for the entire Sentinel system is planned by March 2027. The Air Force asked for almost $540 million to fund Mk21A reentry vehicle development in the fiscal 2027 budget request, up $184 million from 2026 as Sentinel ramps up integration and test activities.

articles.title: In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
articles.body:
In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

articles.title: Record Zircon Barrage Targets Kyiv as Russia Fires 39 Ballistic Missiles at Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Record Zircon Barrage Targets Kyiv as Russia Fires 39 Ballistic Missiles at Ukraine
Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukraine overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, while monitoring channels reported a record barrage of roughly 25 Zircon missiles aimed at Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Russian strikes on energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv left at least 600,000 people without electricity, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 14.
The Ukrainian President described the barrage as a deliberate strike on energy infrastructure that he said was specifically covered by a ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump. Zelenskyy argued that the scale of the operation represented an unusually open challenge to Washington.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Overnight, the Russians used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv. A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure—the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s Air Force said air defenses neutralized 115 UAVs and four ballistic missiles during the barrage. The strikes nevertheless caused extensive damage, with Zelenskyy saying 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four oil and gas facilities were affected.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale—Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States. Russia does not consider the American President’s statements strong,” Zelenskyy added.
Ukrainian monitoring channels also reported that Russia used a record number of Zircon missiles during the attack, with roughly 25 reportedly launched against targets in Kyiv and the Kyiv region. Ukraine’s Air Force has not yet officially confirmed the figure.
“Unfortunately, at least 600,000 people are now without power. Outages could become even more widespread. Unfortunately, there is significant damage to facilities and equipment—at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector,” Zelenskyy stated.
He thanked repair crews, energy workers, and emergency personnel responding across the affected regions, adding that the strikes had caused deaths and injuries.
In Kyiv, the number of injured rose to 25. Among them was a 7-year-old girl in the Desnianskyi district who suffered cuts and burns to her hand.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, two people were killed and six others injured, while a business in Dnipro was damaged. Two more people were wounded in the Khmelnytskyi region, where a gas station was hit and a fire broke out at an industrial facility.
That brings the confirmed toll from the locations reported so far to at least two dead and 33 injured.
Zelenskyy called for a forceful international response, arguing that Moscow had rejected an opportunity for de-escalation.
“We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond—and to respond forcefully. Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” he said.
The Ukrainian leader specifically appealed to Trump to impose stronger sanctions on Russia, pointing to recently enacted legislation backed by US Sen. Lindsey Graham.
“We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures. The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor,” the Ukrainian President wrote.
He also renewed Ukraine’s request for additional Patriot interceptor missiles as Russia expands its use of ballistic weapons, which are among the most difficult threats for Ukrainian air defenses to stop.
“We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine. It is entirely fair for us to tell the United States, Europe, and all our partners that no country in the world should be left alone to face such a deranged and pro-war actor as Russia,” Zelenskyy concluded.
Earlier, the Ukrainian President stated that Ukraine has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities for two consecutive days following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, while Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
