articles.title: Russia launches 39 missiles, 128 UAVs at Ukraine; 4 missiles, 115 drones downed or suppressed – Air Force
articles.body:
Russian forces on Wednesday overnight deployed 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types against Ukraine, of which air defense forces shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 UAVs, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"On the night of October 14 (from 18:00 on October 13), the enemy launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine using strike UAVs and 39 missiles of various types approaching targets on a ballistic trajectory," the Air Force said in a message on Telegram.
In total, the radio-technical troops of the Air Force recorded 167 air attack weapons – 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types.
According to preliminary data as of 09:00, air defense shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 enemy UAVs, including 59 jet-powered drones. According to the Air Force, this accounts for 90% of the total number of strike UAVs.
Russian forces used Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Oniks missiles, as well as Shahed strike drones, including jet-powered ones, Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera, Italmas, and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The main directions of the strike were Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv region. According to the Air Force, a key feature of the attack was the simultaneous deployment of various air attack weapons from multiple directions, along with a large number of ballistic missiles targeting energy infrastructure facilities.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary information as of 09:00, impacts of missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 22 locations, with falling debris from intercepted targets recorded at eight locations. Some Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
As of the time of publication, the attack was ongoing, with Russian strike drones remaining in Ukrainian airspace.

articles.title: Iran and US on brink of war as Russian mediation falters
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran and US on brink of all-out war as Russia fails to break diplomatic deadlock
Diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States remain deadlocked despite continued exchanges of messages and mediation attempts, raising fears of a renewed military confrontation as both sides step up their threats and preparations.
Qatar and Pakistan have continued efforts to bring Tehran and Washington back to the negotiating table, but little progress has been made as tensions escalate in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks on vessels attempting to use non-Iranian shipping routes have increased.
The diplomatic stalemate comes amid growing US threats and reports of a possible Israeli attack on Iran ahead of Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Iran, meanwhile, has placed its military on heightened alert, conducting new missile tests in recent days and threatening to unveil additional weapons.
Tehran has also warned Washington and regional governments that another round of war could trigger retaliation across a wider geographical area, including potential ground incursions.
The renewed fighting between Yemen's Houthi movement and Saudi Arabia has further complicated the regional situation, with observers linking the escalation to the wider confrontation between Iran and the US and Israel.
Russia's mediation efforts falter
Russia entered the diplomatic efforts around a week ago, with the Kremlin announcing that President Vladimir Putin had conveyed Tehran's proposals for ending the war with the United States to US President Donald Trump.
According to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, Putin discussed his forthcoming telephone conversation with Trump during a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan last week, on the sidelines of a summit of Commonwealth of Independent States leaders.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on Monday that Pezeshkian had clearly outlined Tehran's position to Putin, including its seven-day proposal for resolving the conflict and other issues surrounding the negotiations.
However, Baghaei stopped short of describing Russia as a formal mediator.
"Technically speaking, in the strict sense of the word, Pakistan and Qatar are still playing the role of actual mediators between Iran and the United States," he said.
He added that Tehran welcomed diplomatic efforts by friendly countries, noting that consultations with Moscow on the nuclear issue and other matters were longstanding.
Iranian analyst Ali Gholhaki told The New Arab that Russian diplomacy was proceeding with "weak and lacklustre steps".
He argued that Moscow was attempting to link efforts to resolve the Iran-US conflict with negotiations over the Russia-Ukraine war, hoping that both disputes could be addressed simultaneously.
This, he suggested, explained Russia's more active diplomatic involvement.
Gholhaki said Iran had demonstrated flexibility, but warned that the current regional military positioning suggested another war was considerably more likely than a diplomatic settlement.
He said a new wave of military escalation could erupt at any moment, although Washington appeared reluctant to become embroiled in a full-scale war before the US congressional midterm elections in November.
According to Gholhaki, the Trump administration would prefer to postpone any expansion of the military confrontation until after the vote.
What could another Iran-US war look like?
Iranian military analyst Mehdi Bakhtiari told TNA that another war was a strong possibility, although he expected any confrontation to be relatively short and extremely intense.
He argued that Washington might attempt another military campaign to secure concessions from Tehran and overcome the strategic difficulties it had encountered in its confrontation with Iran.
Bakhtiari said the US and Israel had already fought two wars against Iran, inflicting substantial damage and losses but failing, in his assessment, to achieve their strategic objectives.
Instead, he argued, they had encountered new challenges, particularly the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting rise in global energy and fuel prices.
He suggested that another military campaign could differ significantly from previous confrontations, with attacks potentially concentrating on Iranian nuclear facilities and the country's southern regions.
A central objective, he said, would likely be securing the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Bakhtiari also warned that Iran had prepared new military strategies for such a scenario.
These could include intensified attacks on US naval vessels, particularly destroyers, following incidents in recent weeks in which Iranian forces had fired towards American warships.
He also raised the possibility of Iranian attacks against a larger number of US military bases across the region, particularly in the United Arab Emirates.
According to Bakhtiari, Iranian military planners believe that targeting US interests in the UAE could significantly increase the costs of further escalation for Washington.
He said Iran's military establishment had spent recent weeks rebuilding its missile and air defence capabilities in preparation for a potential confrontation at sea.
Bakhtiari added that both Iran's political elite and wider public increasingly regarded another round of fighting as likely.
Deep divisions over terms for peace
Masoud Foroughi, former editor-in-chief of the conservative Iranian newspaper Farhikhtegan, said the approaching US and Israeli elections were closely connected to calculations about the military confrontation with Iran.
Speaking to TNA, he argued that the war had not ended in the conventional sense but had instead changed its form and geographical scope.
From Tehran's perspective, he said, the conflict would end only when Washington accepted that military force could not fundamentally alter Iran's political system or its behaviour.
Washington, by contrast, was seeking what he described as Iran's complete surrender, whether through military pressure or diplomacy.
Foroughi said the gap between the two sides' demands was so wide that negotiations under current conditions were unlikely to bridge it.
He compared the situation to two parties standing 50 kilometres apart without any means of communication, arguing that even a distance of one kilometre would be too great for them to hear one another.
As a result, he said, the outcome would continue to depend largely on developments on the ground and each side's political, economic and social ability to withstand pressure.
Foroughi argued that the increasingly aggressive rhetoric from Washington and Tehran was intended to influence each other's strategic calculations.
Regardless of whether Trump intended to launch another direct military campaign before the November elections, he said, the administration was seeking to maintain sufficient pressure to force Iran to reconsider its position.
He concluded that diplomacy would only become effective when the costs of continuing the war became sufficiently high to compel Washington to halt its military campaign.

articles.title: Ukraine-NATO AI built to forecast Russia’s front-line drone attacks from past data and weather is ready to plug into the army
articles.body:
Ukraine and NATO have unveiled two artificial intelligence (AI) tools in Vilnius, Lithuania, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on 13 October. One forecasts Russian drone attacks near the front and is ready to join the Armed Forces’ situational awareness systems. The other helps plan artillery fire and is still in testing.
A forecast of where, when, and which drones will fly targets the main source of losses near the front. In March, Ukraine’s military put the share of front-line casualties caused by FPV drones at up to 80%. In May, Ukraine’s drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said Russia was copying Ukraine’s model to grow its drone forces. A month earlier, Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov wrote that adding more drones no longer fundamentally changes the battlefield. The next stage, he said, is full integration of AI.
Forecasting Russian drone attacks
The NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center (JATEC) presented both at a three-day seminar in the Lithuanian capital. NATO’s Allied Command Transformation and Ukraine’s Armed Forces built the tools with JATEC’s support.
“The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems,” the ministry said.
Model No. 13 works from past data, weather, and the current battlefield situation. The ministry said it can identify the intensity of attacks, the areas, the time windows, and the types of drones with a high probability.
Ranking artillery options
Model No. 32 is a decision-support module. It tests whether artillery plans can be generated automatically. It weighs the mission’s requirements and current operational data, including available weapons, ammunition, firing positions, and constraints.
Ukraine’s new military AI does more than watch the battlefield—it helps commanders plan what comes next
First, it applies logistics, ballistics, and impact-zone parameters to throw out unworkable options. Then it scores and ranks the rest. That means less hand-based comparison, faster decisions, and a more efficient fire loop, the ministry said. The prototype is now with the Ukrainian military for trials. If the trials succeed and it is validated, it could be expanded to other units that strike Russian forces.

- NATO country that pays for Kyiv’s Starlink warns Musk as his cap breaks Ukraine’s drone missions: “As your European customers, we are watching you”

articles.title: North Korea Test-Fires KN-30 Missile 910 km, Having Previously Supplied Such Missiles to Russia
articles.body:
North Korea launched a KN-30 ballistic missile on October 12, flying more than 910 km. North Korea had previously supplied Russia with missiles of this model.
North Korea’s state news agency KCNA reported the launch and published photographs.
According to Yonhap, the secretary-general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum identified the missile in the photographs of the five-axle launchers as the Hwasong-11Da-2.5, also known by its Western designation, KN-30.
It is a North Korean solid-fuel, short-range ballistic missile with a reported warhead weight of 2.5 tonnes.
Militarnyi previously reported that North Korea launched at least two ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan on October 12. According to Japan’s Ministry of Defense, one missile flew approximately 220 km, while the other traveled more than 910 km and reached a maximum altitude of around 70 km.
KCNA reported that the test aimed to assess upgrades to key components of the missile systems.
However, Pyongyang did not disclose which components had been upgraded, nor did it officially identify the missile model tested or its flight range.
Russia has reportedly received KN-30 ballistic missiles from North Korea, which it could potentially use to strike Ukraine.
The transfer was reported on August 20, after the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine responded to a request from journalists at Ukrainska Pravda. According to the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine, as of July 2026, Russia had approximately 50 North Korean KN-23, KN-24, and KN-30 ballistic missiles combined.
Russian forces have previously used North Korean KN-23 and KN-24 missiles to strike Ukraine. However, there is currently no confirmed information that KN-30 missiles have been used in combat against Ukraine.
Read more details on the development of North Korea’s missile capabilities and Russia’s role in the process in Militarnyi’s article titled “North Korea’s Missile Program with Russian Support: A New Threat to the US and Its Allies.”
KN-30 is the Western designation for the North Korean Hwasong-11C ballistic missile, also known as the Hwasong-11Da. It is an enlarged version of the Hwasong-11 missile family. The missile is powered by a solid-propellant rocket motor and is launched from a mobile ground-based launcher mounted on a five-axle wheeled chassis.
North Korea first publicly presented the KN-30 at a military parade in Pyongyang on January 14, 2021. Its first known test launches took place on March 25 of the same year. At the time, North Korea claimed the missile had a range of 600 km, although Japanese and South Korean military authorities detected a flight distance of approximately 420–450 km.
North Korea has stated that the missile can be equipped with a warhead weighing 2.5 tonnes. However, this claim has not yet been independently confirmed.

articles.title: Zelenskyy on overnight attack: Russia has never shown such disrespect for America
articles.body:
Zelenskyy on overnight attack: Russia has never shown such disrespect for America
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Russia had shown unprecedented contempt for the United States by carrying out a ballistic missile strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure facilities overnight on 13-14 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy said that Russian forces had used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions on Ukraine's energy and critical infrastructure facilities in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast and Kharkiv.
Quote: "A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President. The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States. Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong."
Details: Zelenskyy wrote that at least 600,000 people are currently without electricity and the number affected could be even higher.
"We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond – and to respond forcefully. Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation. We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorises and regulates such measures," he said.
Zelenskyy added that US President Donald Trump has all the necessary powerful tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice and pressure on Russia.
He has also called for additional interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
"It is entirely fair for us to tell the United States, Europe, and all our partners that no country in the world should be left alone to face such a deranged and pro-war actor as Russia," Zelenskyy added.
Background:
- Trump claimed that the "energy ceasefire" he had announced between Ukraine and Russia is in effect and said reports of violations needed to be checked.
- On 11 October, Trump claimed on his social media platform Truth Social that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire.
- The Kremlin said it had nothing to say about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump.

articles.title: Burnham says UK to increase supply of anti-drone missiles to Ukraine, ahead of PMQs and Zelenskyy meeting – UK politics live
articles.body:
Burnham praises Zelenskyy for showing 'leadership' after Trump's energy ceasefire comment
Here are fuller quotes from the public statements by Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy before their main meeting.
Burnham said:
MrPresident, it’s a great privilege for me to welcome you to Downing Street today. And you’ve just seen the reaction [a reference to the crowd cheering as he arrived]. Obviously, you’ve seen the solidarity and the support you’ve got from everybody here in Britain. We’re behind you. And that will not change.
We know that the last few days, the last few hours, have been very dark and difficult days for Ukraine. We know that the country sustained heavy bombardments in the last 24 hours in Kyiv, particularly. And we would want to extend our condolences to all of those people in Ukraine who’ve lost loved ones as a result of what has been happening.
President Trump made a call at the weekend for an energy ceasefire. And, Volodymyr, you have shown your leadership in saying that you would be prepared to sit down and discuss what that looks like, to make sure we protect people from a very harsh winter that lies ahead in Ukraine.
Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine. It’s clear to the world, again, who the aggressor is in this conflict.
However, in these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support that we can. And today I’m announcing that we are accelerating the delivery of British-made air defences for you, and we will make sure that they’re in place as soon as possible. (See 9am.)
I’ve also asked all of our ministers here in the government to do whatever they can, extra, to support you, and they are looking at all possible avenues …
All of the people of Ukraine have our support. There are such connections between our two countries. We will forever stand by you through this difficult time.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, is holding talks with Andy Burnham in No 10 now, where he said he would be discussing with the PM “difficulties” caused by Ukraine getting less intelligence and reduced access to the Starlink internet access in the light of Washington striking a diesel deal with Russia. (See 5.31pm.)
Andy Burnham has ruled out Labour doing deals with the Green party after its conference voted for a motion saying “Zionism is racism”. (See 12.57pm.)
Dominic Cummings has not received much coverage for his appearance at the Lords constitution committee this morning, where he was talking about constitutional safeguards, and I’ve afraid I have too much other stuff on to give it much attention. But if you want to listen to a better expert on the constitution, Peter Hennessy, the historian and crossbencher peer, has given an interview to the Lord Speaker’s Corner podcast. The transcript and audio are here.
Hennessy said constitutional safeguards could quickly crumble. He said:
So much would go wrong.
If we had a government that came in, if it was a Reform government, and the first thing they did was sack the cabinet secretary, and got rid of the career officials who came in under the Northcote-Trevelyan merit, not partisanship rubric of selection, and had a go at the judges, too – it would be very easy if they had a big enough majority for them to take away the fundamentals … as the first act that they were doing week one.
We have a major competitor for power now in this country who said what they’d do. In effect, they would rip up the constitution, and the way we recruit and promote our senior civil servants, and indeed would interfere in the choice of judges.
And so much would go … We’d crumble, and it would be very hard to get it back.
Government says 900,000 people could get stronger rights under crackdown on bogus self-employment loopholes
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has told published a consultation paper on employment status reform. This sets out how the government proposes to implement plans he announced at Labour conference to close the “bogus self-employment loopholes” that deny workers basic rights.
Explaining the plans, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade says:
Bogus self-employment is a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations.
However, the day-to-day reality is that many of these people are treated as workers, not self-employed. External estimates suggest that as many as 900,000 people may currently be affected by this and could be missing out on core employment rights.
The proposals to be consulted on could provide greater clarity to businesses and workers, levelling the playing field for those businesses who are already doing the right thing and clamping down on abuses. This could help workers such as parcel couriers, delivery drivers, hairdressers and gig economy workers.
But, in a good article on this topic for LabourList, Tom Berger points out that the plans don’t include a firm commitment to create a single status of worker in employment law – something that in opposition the party did commit to.
Meri Ahlberg, a senior policy adviser at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, a thinktank that has argued for employment status reform, said:
The measures in the government’s consultation are a step forward for making sure people have the rights and protections everyone deserves. But without putting single worker status and tax reform on the table for the near future, it will still be cheaper to employ people in less secure jobs and millions of workers will be left without sick pay and parental pay. It’s time basic protections were in place for everyone, however they work, and that existing protections are enforced properly.
Zelenskyy says he will be discussing intelligence sharing 'difficulties' and Starlink access with Burnham
And this is what Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, said in reply to Andy Burnham.
We are very thankful, all our people in Ukraine, we absolutely thankful to your nation. You are strong people, a very supportive nation …
[This is a] terrible war. Absolutely terrible as.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was being attacked by ballistic missiles and hundreds of Iranian drones.
There was no energy ceasefire, he said. It looked like “escalation from Russian side”.
He said he wanted the war to stop.
We have massive attacks today, and it’s a pity that we had also some difficulties. What I want to discuss with Andy – about Starlink and about intelligence. There are lot of different surprises on which you can’t count.
He said UK was one of Ukraine’s strongest partners.
A reporter asked Zelenskyy if he could confirm that the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, and if it had slowed down Starlink – meaning Ukrainian weapons lose access to the internet at very high speeds (making them inoperable). Zelenskyy did not answer.
Burnham praises Zelenskyy for showing 'leadership' after Trump's energy ceasefire comment
Here are fuller quotes from the public statements by Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy before their main meeting.
Burnham said:
MrPresident, it’s a great privilege for me to welcome you to Downing Street today. And you’ve just seen the reaction [a reference to the crowd cheering as he arrived]. Obviously, you’ve seen the solidarity and the support you’ve got from everybody here in Britain. We’re behind you. And that will not change.
We know that the last few days, the last few hours, have been very dark and difficult days for Ukraine. We know that the country sustained heavy bombardments in the last 24 hours in Kyiv, particularly. And we would want to extend our condolences to all of those people in Ukraine who’ve lost loved ones as a result of what has been happening.
President Trump made a call at the weekend for an energy ceasefire. And, Volodymyr, you have shown your leadership in saying that you would be prepared to sit down and discuss what that looks like, to make sure we protect people from a very harsh winter that lies ahead in Ukraine.
Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine. It’s clear to the world, again, who the aggressor is in this conflict.
However, in these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support that we can. And today I’m announcing that we are accelerating the delivery of British-made air defences for you, and we will make sure that they’re in place as soon as possible. (See 9am.)
I’ve also asked all of our ministers here in the government to do whatever they can, extra, to support you, and they are looking at all possible avenues …
All of the people of Ukraine have our support. There are such connections between our two countries. We will forever stand by you through this difficult time.
Burnham tells Zelenskyy's UK's support for Ukraine 'will not change'
Andy Burnham told Volodymyr Zelenskyy Britain’s support for Ukraine “will not change”, as he welcomed the leader to Downing Street.
In public remarks before their main meeting got under way, Burnham said:
You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change.
He added that recent days had been “dark and difficult” for Ukraine, which has suffered “heavy bombardment in the last 24 hours”, and he extending the UK’s condolences to those who had lost loved ones.
Burnham said Zelenskyy was “prepared to sit down and discuss” the energy ceasefire proposed by Donald Trump, but added: “Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine.”
He said:
In these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support we can.
Zelenskyy said he was “thankful” for British support, saying:
Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I’m very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it’s your people, Andy.
Andy Burnham has welcomed President Zelenskyy to Downing Street.
As they posed for pictures outside No 10, there was a loud cheer from Foreign Office staff who were there watching. (The Foreign Office is next door to Downing Street.)
King Charles meets Zelenskyy, before Ukrainian president's meeting with Burnham
Another ‘show of support’ feature of President Zelenskyy’s visit is the fact that he was invited to meet the king at Buckingham Palace. Foreign leaders coming to Downing Street for a political visit don’t normally get to meet the king at the same time. But Charles and Zelenskyy have met many times before, and the king is a strong supporter of Ukraine.
Thank you to His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. For me, it is important to have the opportunity to personally thank him for the unwavering support of Ukraine. We appreciate all the assistance from the United Kingdom.
While Andy Burnham has been relatively guarded in what he has said in public (see 12.40pm) about Donald Trump buying diesel from Russia and declaring that Volodymyr Zelenskyy should be replaced as Ukrainian president, this is a way of using the apparatus of the state to send a visual signal that the UK is very, very firmly on Zelenskyy’s side on this one.
President Zelenskyy is expected to arrive in Downing Street shortly. Unusually, there will be a ceremonial military guard there to greet him. According to Sky News, Downing Street has not laid on one of these for a visitor since Donald Trump visited Chequers.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia attacked with 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones; energy infrastructure was targeted

Unfortunately, there is significant damage to facilities and equipment at 26 elements of our power system and at four facilities of the oil and gas complex. I am grateful to the repair crews, all Ukrainian power engineers, and employees of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine for all their efforts to eliminate the consequences of this Russian strike. Unfortunately, there are casualties and injuries

We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to respond—and to respond harshly. articles.title: Kyiv Mayor Faces Questioning as Russian Attack Triggers Fresh Water Cuts
articles.body:
Kyiv is experiencing water supply issues once more on Wednesday after another Russian attack on Ukraine’s energy grid.
The attack, comprising ballistic missiles, hit Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a nine-story residential building, killing at least three and injuring 26.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kyiv City State Administration reported reduced water pressure in multiple districts as a result of the attack, with reduced voltage preventing the pumps from operating normally.
“Due to the power outage of some water supply facilities in the capital, the pumping equipment was stopped in an emergency,” it wrote in a statement, adding that restoration work is ongoing.
According to the agency, the upper half of the Pecherskyi district has no water, while the lower part has reduced pressure. The Solomyansky and Shevchenkivskyi districts also suffer from reduced pressure.
State media Ukrinform noted that Kyivvodfond, a municipal water-management firm, has developed an online map of available manual water pumps around Kyiv.
In October, the capital reported multiple water outages caused by Russian attacks, two months ahead of the cold spell. Most Ukrainians interviewed by Kyiv Post on Tuesday named water disruptions as their top concern for the upcoming winter, as signs of an energy truce touted by Washington remain elusive, with Ukraine’s energy grid not included.
Kyiv also said it was not warned by its allies for the first wave of ballistic missile strikes amid rumors of a US intelligence cutoff.
Ukraine’s Business Leaders to Tackle War Risks and Economic Resilience at 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum on Oct. 26
Kyiv authorities urged locals to stock up on food and water on Sunday, Oct. 11, after a Russian attack left over half of Kyiv’s households without running water.
Kyiv mayor summoned
On Wednesday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko was summoned to the Verkhovna Rada to answer questions about the city’s readiness for Russian attacks on power facilities.
The session is ongoing at the time of publication, and it was preceded by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s criticism of Kyiv’s response to the impending energy crisis, arguing that the capital trails behind other regions in preparedness.
However, Klitschko has defended the city’s preparedness, noting that progress is being made through backup systems despite limited funding, as facilities can’t be fully shielded without adequate air defense.
The standoff is also part of a longstanding animosity between the two that predates Russia’s full-scale invasion.

articles.title: “He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow
articles.body:
Washington is pressing the victim, not the aggressor, a Ukrainian diplomat says. President Donald Trump is using the threat of cutting military aid and intelligence as a tool to pressure Ukraine, while failing to apply enough pressure on Russia to stop the war, says Oleksandr Khara, executive director of the Center for Defense Strategies, Espreso reports.
Ukraine’s drones and air defense still lean on US satellite intelligence and weapons, which gives Trump room to squeeze Kyiv rather than Moscow. Khara argues Trump wants to end the war on Ukraine’s and Europe’s account to restore normal relations with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, treating Ukraine as the weak link to be pushed.
“Trump wants to use restrictions, levers of influence on Ukraine to achieve his goal. To end or stop this war at any cost, at the expense of Ukraine and Europe, to restore normal relations with Putin,” Khara said.
Using American aid as leverage over Kyiv is not new for Trump, the diplomat noted, recalling earlier instances in which support was blocked or suspended.
The pressure points Trump picks, and the ones he leaves alone
Trump wants a visible success in ending the war, Khara says, partly against the backdrop of US domestic politics. He has economic tools to press Moscow but is in no hurry to use them, and his administration is instead gradually loosening sanctions on Russia.
“He doesn’t want to pressure Russia. He thinks Ukraine is the weak link and that it needs to be pushed,” Khara stressed.
Ukraine’s dependence on US support has fallen thanks to European partners, he added, so Kyiv has more room to keep fighting even as European states keep buying American weapons for it.
The one trade Kyiv might accept, and the pressure until then
An energy ceasefire is possible only on strict terms, Khara believes. Kyiv could agree to stop striking Russian refineries only if Moscow halts attacks on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission, heating, and the Black Sea ports and the ships heading to them.
Until such a deal exists, Ukraine must hit harder, he argued, because steadily draining Russia’s economic resources is what could force the Kremlin to reconsider.
“As long as there is no such agreement, and no desire from Russia, we must increase this pressure and destroy as much of their energy infrastructure as possible,” Khara said.

- “Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
- “Trump was looking for any opportunity to undermine our defense capabilities,” top Ukrainian volunteer, who supplied 291,502 FPV drones to front, says of sudden Starlink limit

articles.title: Ukrainian military says SpaceX restricted Starlink terminals without warning
articles.body:
Ukrainian military says SpaceX restricted Starlink terminals without warning
SpaceX has restricted the Starlink satellite communication terminals used by Ukrainian troops at the front, slowing the drones that rely on them, according to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, and Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the Ukrainian defense minister and a volunteer.
The news outlet Ukrainska Pravda, citing the military, reported that the restrictions targeted Starshield, the faster military version of Starlink used by drone operators. One commander sent the outlet a video showing two Ukrainian drones climbing into the sky with their connection “dropping out,” leaving them unable to continue their mission.
A source in the Ukrainian Armed Forces told Ukrainska Pravda that standard Starlink terminals installed on drones work at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (99 mph), but that speed is not enough for some missions, which is why drone operators use Starshield, the military version of Starlink.
“Our defense forces did not receive any warning about these restrictions, and it led to the failure of a number of missions. It’s obvious that this action can’t be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” Beskrestnov wrote.
Volodymyr Zelensky said over the past two days that Western partners did not warn Ukraine about missile strikes on Kyiv. The United States told Ukraine it had not shared intelligence because of poor weather conditions, according to Politico.
The United States threatened last week to halt intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block arms deliveries unless Kyiv agreed to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, according to reporting from the Financial Times.

articles.title: Chinese company 'helping Houthis' improve missile capabilities
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Chinese company 'helping Houthis' improve missile capabilities as fears grow for civilians in Taiz
Yemen's Houthis are trying to manufacture their own ballistic missiles, reportedly using components delivered by a Chinese company, according to information obtained by Conflict Armament Research.
The Iran-backed group has bought a range of parts from a Chinese supplier and is attempting to locally produce Tehran's Kheibar Shekan missile, a cheap, precision-guided projectile that can evade air defences.
The Conflict Armament Research report says the missile would have a range of around 1,200 miles, enabling the group to launch strikes across the Gulf, Israel, Jordan and most of Egypt.
This is one of the first indications that the group is pursuing an advanced indigenous weapons programme independently of Iran.
The report was based on information given by Yemeni authorities in July after officials intercepted two shipments last year.
China has also emerged as one of Iran's biggest suppliers of dual-use components during its war with the US and Israel.
Customs data has shown hundreds of shipments have been delivered to Iran's defence ministry in recent months, providing it a vital lifeline to maintain military production during the war.
Advance on Taiz
The Houthis continued to advance towards Taiz on Tuesday, capturing the western entrance to the city.
The country's third-largest city is a major stronghold of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government's and has been a battleground since the long-running conflict was reignited in September amid the US-Iran war.
A Houthi offensive last week saw the group encircle the city, severing its last remaining supply lines.
Military sources told Reuters that clashes were ongoing in al-Dabab, 10 km from Taiz, and on Sabr Mountain, which overlooks the southern edge of the city.
Yemeni warplanes targeted Houthi forces in Dabab and Misrakh south of the city, government forces said in a statement on Tuesday.
Civilian casualties in the city are also mounting as the Houthis advance closer to the city. Yemen's internationally recognised government said Houthi shelling and drone attacks on Monday were responsible for the deaths of at least six people, including a child, and the wounding of another 17 in the city.
It accused the group of shelling residential areas of the city, damaging seven buildings.
Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media said one woman was killed and four others injured in an airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition outside the city.
Fears for civilians amid siege
Yemeni civilians in Taiz are facing a "devastating" humanitarian crisis as Houthi forces step up their attacks on the blockaded city, the UN has warned.
"We're alarmed by the intense hostilities across multiple front lines, particularly in Taiz, which is having devastating humanitarian consequences for civilians," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said at a press briefing on Tuesday.
He warned that the blockade was beginning to cause shortages and drive up the prices of goods. Wheat and flour supplies could run out in less than three weeks, he said.
Dwindling fuel supplies are beginning to affect the water supply, risking water shortages for the estimated one million people who live in the city.
The World Health Organisation on Tuesday warned that the war is causing a resurgence in cholera. One quarter of the 8000 cases declared this year have occurred in the past four weeks alone, it said.
The resumption of the conflict last month has triggered a renewed humanitarian crisis across much of the country, displacing hundreds of thousands of people and putting millions at risk of famine.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes a Sberbank data center in Russia. Meanwhile, Kyiv isn’t getting crucial missile warnings from the U.S., and SpaceX is restricting Starlink.
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes a Sberbank data center in Russia. Meanwhile, Kyiv isn’t getting crucial missile warnings from the U.S., and SpaceX is restricting Starlink.
Russia
Ukrainian drones struck a data center operated by Sberbank in the city of Balakovo in the Saratov region overnight on October 14. Ukrainian monitoring channels were the first to report the attack. Saratov Governor Roman Busargin said the strike damaged residential buildings in Balakovo and killed one person. He said all infrastructure facilities in the city are “operating normally.”
A few hours later, Sberbank First Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin confirmed the attack on the data center, saying all the bank’s systems and services are “operating normally.” The bank’s press service said no employees were injured.
This is the first Ukrainian attack on Sberbank data centers. Last week, Ukrainian drones struck data centers belonging to Yandex in the Ryazan and Vladimir regions, as well as in Kaluga.
Sberbank announced plans to build a data center in the Saratov region in 2020 and began construction the following year. The facility is expected to cover almost 60,000 square meters (about 646,000 square feet). Authorities said it would be the largest data center in Europe, and one of Sberbank’s supercomputers is being built at the Balakovo site.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s Western partners once again failed to warn Kyiv that Russia was preparing a ballistic missile strike on the capital, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the evening of October 13. He said the missiles were detected only as they approached Kyiv. The main target was the CHP-4 power plant, one of Kyiv’s major energy facilities.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said partners did not warn Ukraine ahead of the first ballistic missile strike during the overnight attack on October 14, but did send notifications ahead of the three subsequent waves of strikes.
A day earlier, Zelensky had said Ukraine had received no intelligence from Western partners about the Russian missile strike on Kyiv on October 12. “Intelligence about the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save people’s lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is exactly what helps prevent killings when there is a warning about ballistic missiles,” he said.
According to Politico, the United States told Ukraine it had withheld intelligence about the missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of October 12 because of poor weather conditions. Ukrainian authorities fear “this might not have been the case.”
U.S. President Donald Trump, asked directly by a journalist whether Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, answered: “No.” Earlier, the Financial Times reported that the United States had threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
On the morning of October 14, Ukrainian military personnel began reporting that SpaceX had restricted the operation of Starlink satellite terminals used by Ukrainian forces at the front. The restrictions affect Starshield, the military version of Starlink, and limit the speed of drones that rely on satellite communications.
Starshield is faster and necessary for drone operators, a source in the Ukrainian military told Ukrainska Pravda, a Ukrainian news outlet. Regular Starlink, installed on drones, supports speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (99 mph), which is not enough for some missions. One commander sent the outlet a video showing two Ukrainian drones climbing into the sky and then “lose” their connection, unable to continue the mission.
“Our defense forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and that led to the failure of a number of missions. It’s obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president.
SpaceX has not yet commented on the Ukrainian military’s statements.
The war in photos. The aftermath of the missile strike on Kyiv
Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring 21, according to the latest data. A strike hit a multistory residential building in the Desnianskyi district. Among the injured is a child.

articles.title: The Kremlin’s faction in the European Parliament: Meet the MEPs still traveling to Russia to meet politicians, officials and even spies
articles.body:
On Oct. 8, in the wake of Russia’s nationwide legislative elections, the European Parliament overwhelmingly declared the resulting State Duma in Moscow to be illegitimate — the result of a stage-managed “vote” that was neither free nor fair. Nevertheless, 42 European lawmakers voted against what might have seemed to be an obvious resolution. Even after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the European Parliament’s faction of so-called Putinversteher — a German term meaning people who profess to “understand Putin” (and often rationalize Kremlin policies) — remains firmly in place. They continue to travel to Russia, repeat Kremlin narratives, and meet with Kremlin officials and intelligence officers involved in managing foreign influence networks.
The Insider found that one in 10 current members of the European Parliament has visited Russia since the annexation of Crimea in 2014, and at least two dozen of them can be described as openly pro-Kremlin.
“Che Guevara” visits the Foreign Intelligence Service
In April of 2026, Slovak member of the European Parliament Ľuboš Blaha walked through the Russian State Duma building to a song by the band Lyube and denounced what he called Western hypocrisy. Blaha knows something about political symbolism: while serving as deputy speaker of Slovakia’s parliament, he removed the EU flag from his office and hung a portrait of the Argentinean-born Cuban revolutionary leader Che Guevara. A year later, he was elected to the European Parliament, where he receives a salary of around 10,000 euros a month.
An ally of Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, Blaha visited the State Duma as part of a trip he officially reported as having been organized by the Russian Historical Society — which happens to be chaired by Sergei Naryshkin, the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
Although there is no indication that Blaha and Naryshkin saw one another this time around, during a 2025 visit to Moscow the two did indeed meet. Notably, unlike in the case of Blaha’s other travels to Russia, that 2025 trip was not reported on the European Parliament’s website. The trip is nevertheless confirmed both by the politician’s own social media posts and by flight data obtained by The Insider.
During the 2025 excursion, the MEP also met with lawmaker Leonid Slutsky, who has been implicated in efforts to recruit foreigners, as well as with Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov. Blaha presents himself as a left-wing politician and makes a point of highlighting that identity during his trips to Russia — for example by sending a “heartfelt revolutionary greeting” from a Lenin monument in Sochi.
It is unclear what a self-described socialist finds so appealing about Russia, where economic inequality recently reached a record level. Nor did Blaha appear troubled by the fact that Naryshkin, at whose invitation he travels to Russia to criticize the West, is financially supported by oligarch God Nisanov.
Malofeev’s operative and a lobbyist for criminal oligarchs
French member of the European Parliament Thierry Mariani is a favorite of Kremlin propaganda. Russian state news agencies quote him almost as often as they do Russian officials. TASS, for example, obtains comments from Mariani directly. He has called a Ukrainian strike on the Panorama museum in Russian-occupied Sevastopol unacceptable, criticized financial aid to Ukraine, and called for ending the war on Russia’s terms. The French politician has long and consistently sided with Russian authorities. He even criticized Alexei Navalny while the opposition leader was still alive in prison.
Mariani’s wife is known to be originally from Russia. Publicly, the Yekaterinburg native has appeared either under her maiden name, Shaikhullina, or as Irina Mariani. In official documents, however, The Insider found that she uses the surname of her former husband, Ivanko.
Officially, Irina Ivanko did not work anywhere before meeting Mariani at a Moscow restaurant and moving to Paris in the 2000s. She is now 50 and is raising their son. Her brother, Sergei Presnetsov (formerly Shaikhullin) remained in Russia. From 2023 to 2025, he served as deputy head of the administration of Verkhnyaya Pyshma in Russia’s Sverdlovsk Region.
The brother of the French politician’s wife works for the Ural Mining and Metallurgical Company (UMMC), which is controlled by the oligarchs Andrei Bokarev and Iskander Makhmudov, both of whom have interests in France. Makhmudov has also appeared as a partner of the Franco-Russian Dialogue association, which is headed by Mariani. Former Russian Railways CEO Vladimir Yakunin is also closely linked to the group.
In 2021, French authorities opened two preliminary investigations into Mariani over his involvement with the Franco-Russian Dialogue. He was suspected of corruption, breach of trust, and money laundering, as well as influence peddling; questions were also raised over whether certain benefits, suspicious financial transactions, and trips may have been compensation for his maintenance of political positions favorable to the Kremlin.
French authorities investigated Mariani on suspicion of corruption, breach of trust, and money laundering
The Franco-Russian Dialogue was created in 2004 under the patronage of Vladimir Putin and then-French President Jacques Chirac. Despite allegations that the group was politically aligned with Moscow, Mariani continued making frequent trips to Russia through at least 2024.
Leaked documents also show that paperwork for Mariani’s visit to the 2018 World Cup in Russia was handled by Maria Reshetova, an aide to Konstantin Malofeev. Malofeev, often described in Russia as an “Orthodox oligarch” because of his ultraconservative religious politics, has long overseen foreign influence networks working on the Kremlin’s behalf.
Reshetova also handled World Cup paperwork for other foreign politicians, including French MEP Philippe Olivier, members of the Le Pen family, Austrian lawmaker Johannes Hübner, German far-right publicist Manuel Ochsenreiter, Bulgarian Russophile Nikolay Malinov, Italian political operative Gianluca Savoini, and Serbian lawmaker Boško Obradović.
The French Legion in Putin’s ranks
Former French military intelligence chief Christophe Gomart last visited Russia in 2016, but the effects of that trip appear to have lasted. In 2015, he drew attention for his controversial claim that Russia had supposedly never prepared a military invasion of Ukraine, and after entering the European Parliament, Gomart continued making statements favorable to the Kremlin.
The lawmaker has spoken of the impossibility of securing a Ukrainian victory in the current war and praised what he called Russia’s “deep strategy.” He also urged France not to supply tanks to Kyiv.
Two French members of the European Parliament, Virginie Joron and Catherine Griset, helped give legitimacy to Vladimir Putin’s 2020 vote on constitutional changes, which effectively reset his presidential term count and allowed him to remain in power until at least 2036. They were among the Kremlin-friendly Western politicians who traveled to observe the vote in Russian-annexed Crimea.
Virginie Joron and Catherine Griset helped legitimize Putin’s 2020 constitutional vote extending his path to remain in power
Joron called for avoiding steps that would “add fuel to the fire” in relations with Russia and argued that, instead of sanctions, Europe should seek ways to improve and expand cooperation. She also commented on Alexei Navalny: “If a Frenchman were arrested for such a violation, that would be considered normal.”
Griset, a former personal assistant to Marine Le Pen, was involved in the corruption scandal that saw Le Pen accused of misappropriating European Parliament funds. A few years later, Griset herself won a seat in the European Parliament.
Germany’s “Alternative”
Leaked border service records show that three German members of the European Parliament — Petr Bystron, Markus Buchheit, and Tomasz Froelich — have also traveled to Russia. Froelich continued making such trips through at least 2024.
All three represent the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), reinforcing the party’s reputation for pro-Kremlin positions. Buchheit, for example, opposes sanctions against Russia and is against arms deliveries to Ukraine.
German MEPs Ruth Firmenich and Michael von der Schulenburg also continued traveling to Moscow in 2026.
The Insider has previously reported on how AfD lawmakers received money and assignments from the FSB’s Fifth Service, the branch of Russia’s security service responsible for foreign intelligence operations in the former Soviet space and political influence work.
“Brothers” from Italy
When the European Parliament debated a resolution refusing to recognize Russian elections as free and fair, Italian lawmaker Danilo Della Valle was the first to speak up against it, arguing that Russia has an opposition while citing Yabloko and the Communist Party. He apparently did not know that Yabloko had not been allowed to take part in the election. Della Valle also said Europeans should look at themselves rather than criticize Russia.
Della Valle has long criticized EU policy toward the war in Ukraine. He also defended conductor Valery Gergiev, a longtime associate of Vladimir Putin, when his concerts were canceled. Della Valle traveled frequently to Russia from 2015 to 2019.
Another frequent visitor is Antonio Decaro, the former mayor of the Italian city of Bari. He traveled to Russia while serving as mayor and during that period took part in the opening of an honorary Russian consulate in Bari.
MEP Carlo Fidanza, who represents the Brothers of Italy party, traveled to Russia in 2017 at a time when when he was director-general of Liguria’s tourism promotion agency and worked on attracting Russian tourists. Later, while serving in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, he argued for dialogue with Russia.
Pierfrancesco Maran visited Russia in 2014 and 2018 while serving on Milan’s city council.
Dario Nardella entered the European Parliament in 2024 after previously serving as mayor of Florence. He traveled to Russia in that capacity. At the time, he opposed sanctions against Russia.
Neighborly ties
Some members of the European Parliament from countries that directly border Russia not only continue traveling there, but also openly support narratives favorable to the Kremlin.
Polish MEP Grzegorz Braun recently disrupted a European Parliament appearance by Russian opposition figures. He has called for normalization of relations with Russia and has trampled an EU flag.
Lithuanian MEP Petras Gražulis traveled to Russia from 2015 to 2018 while serving in Lithuania’s national parliament. During those years, he said Lithuania and the European Union should follow Russia’s example in combating what he called “nontraditional” relationships, a phrase commonly used in Russia as a euphemism for LGBTQ relationships.
Gražulis was even accused of bribing Russian officials. He is no stranger to appearing in criminal proceedings, and last year he was stripped of parliamentary immunity.
Estonian MEP Yana Toom makes no secret of traveling to Russia, including during the war. More broadly, she has taken a relatively measured approach to defending the interests of Russian citizens in Estonia and criticizing the Estonian authorities, while also opposing Vladimir Putin and condemning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Three Finnish MEPs have also visited Russia since sanctions were imposed. Eero Heinäluoma traveled there in 2015 and 2016 while serving in Finland’s parliament, where he chaired a “Russia friendship group.” Putin awarded him Russia’s Order of Friendship in 2017. In 2025, Heinäluoma called for dialogue with Russia.
Eero Heinäluoma chaired a Russia friendship group and received Russia’s Order of Friendship from Putin
Katri Kulmuni traveled to Russia from 2016 to 2019 while chairing the Finland-Russia Society. She developed an interest in Russia while still in school; she studied Russian and spent time studying in St. Petersburg. In 2022, however, Russia’s Foreign Ministry severed relations with the Finland-Russia Society, accusing it of taking an “openly anti-Russian position.”
MEP Maria Guzenina also has personal ties to Russia. She is of Russian descent, though she was born in Finland, so her visits to Russia can be explained by family connections.
An Orthodox-Slavic bloc
Among the “Russia enthusiasts,” a sizable group comes from countries generally considered predominantly Slavic, Orthodox Christian, or both.
Bulgarian MEP Petar Volgin has accused EU leaders of Russophobia, saying: “While the leaders of the United States and Russia are trying to stop the war, the European Union is doing everything possible to make sure the war does not end.”
Volgin calls Russia a great country and advocates the “normalization” of relations.
Greek MEP Elena Kountoura traveled to Russia while serving as culture minister in Athens. In the European Parliament, she refused to support the creation of a tribunal to prosecute Russia.
Another Greek lawmaker, Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos, voted against condemning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. He criticized the European Commission for, in his words, lacking money for its own citizens while having billions for Ukraine.
Cypriot TikToker Fidias Panayiotou won a seat in the European Parliament after campaigning to make politics “fashionable, interesting, and closer to the people.” But he has turned out to be closer to Moscow than to Europe, as he traveled to Russia in 2023 and 2025, including for a meeting with State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin. His most recent visit was on May 9, 2025, for Russia's annual Victory Day military parade.
Panayiotou advocates friendly relations with the Russian authorities and has linked that position to his Orthodox Christian faith.
Antonín Staněk of the Czech Republic traveled to Russia while serving as mayor of Olomouc. During that period, he also attended the ceremonial unveiling of a monument to Red Army soldiers in the Czech Republic, appearing alongside Russian representatives. Another Czech MEP, Ondřej Dostál, attended the Victory Day parade in Moscow in 2025.
Branislav Ondruš of Slovakia declined to support a tribunal against Russia. Another Slovak MEP, Milan Uhrík, called in 2024 for the creation of an EU-Russia parliamentary cooperation committee.
To Russia — without love
The Insider also identified several dozen other members of the European Parliament who visited Russia after sanctions were imposed but were not known for openly expressing sympathy for the Kremlin. In some cases, they have indeed been harsh critics of Vladimir Putin. The following MEPs had an opportunity to form their own impressions of Russia from their personal visits there:
- Li Andersson of Finland
- Vytenis Andriukaitis of Lithuania
- François-Xavier Bellamy of France
- Olivier Chastel of Belgium
- Henrik Dahl of Denmark
- Michał Dworczyk of Poland
- Christian Ehler of Germany
- Alma Ezcurra of Spain
- Markus Ferber of Germany
- Borja Giménez Larraz of Spain
- Sunčana Glavak of Croatia
- Małgorzata Gosiewska of Poland
- Hannes Heide of Austria
- Romana Jerković of Croatia
- Reinhold Lopatka of Austria
- César Luena of Spain
- Marit Maij of the Netherlands
- Fulvio Martusciello of Italy
- Liudas Mažylis of Lithuania
- Sven Mikser of Estonia
- Ștefan Mușoiu of Romania
- Hannah Neumann of Germany
- Rasmus Nordqvist of Denmark
- Jüri Ratas of Estonia
- Karlo Ressler of Croatia
- Aura Salla of Finland
- Lena Schilling of Austria
- Raffaele Stancanelli of Italy
- Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann of Germany
- Nils Ušakovs of Latvia
- Brigitte van den Berg of the Netherlands
- Kristian Vigenin of Bulgaria
- Tomáš Zdechovský of the Czech Republic
The Insider sent questions to the lawmakers named above, asking them to disclose details of their trips to Russia. Several had responded by the time the article was published.
Fulvio Martusciello said he had never been to Russia — “I never went there. Never.” However, the Kordon border-crossing database contains a record matching his first and last name, date of birth, and citizenship; it shows that he crossed the Russian border in 2015. According to the record, he flew in from Brussels, spent three days in Moscow, and returned to the Belgian capital. At the time, he was already a member of the European Parliament. Martusciello has been seen supporting Ilan Shor, a pro-Russian Moldovan oligarch. The Italian MEP is now suspected of corrupt ties to Chinese telecommunications company Huawei, and the European Parliament has stripped him of immunity.
Reinhold Lopatka said he traveled to Russia in 2018 as an observer for the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) during the presidential election. He did not disclose another trip in 2021. The Insider confirmed it was the same person as the passport numbers recorded at the border checks in 2018 and 2021 matched.
The office of Nils Ušakovs responded that:
“Mr. N. Ušakovs has been a Member of the European Parliament since July 2019. Throughout his time as a Member, he has made no visits to the Russian Federation: none official, none private. Accordingly, there are no dates, purposes or organisers to report.”
However, according to The Insider’s data, the Latvian MEP’s trips did take place while he was mayor of Riga. Latvia suspects him of corruption offenses committed while in office, but he is protected by parliamentary immunity as an MEP.
Brigitte van den Berg said she traveled to Russia to take intensive language courses.
Markus Ferber offered substantive and informative responses explaining that his visits to Russia in 2016 and 2018 were made in his capacity as deputy chairman of the Hanns Seidel Foundation, not as a member of the European Parliament. Russia now designates the foundation an “undesirable organization,” a legal status used by Russian authorities to ban foreign organizations deemed threatening to the state and to open up opportunities to prosecute people associated with them.
Li Andersson said her trips to Russia were for tourism:
“Yes I have in fact, many years before I became an MEP, been on a few short weekend trips from Helsinki to Saint Petersburg with my friends. I must admit it is so far back that I don't remember the exact dates, but I think it was in 2016 and 2019.
It was nothing official, and was of course paid for by myself.
I haven't been to Russia since then. In recent years I have been on a few trips to Ukraine, to see the horrible damage from Russian attacks with my own eyes.”
Karlo Ressler traveled to Russia for the FIFA World Cup in 2018.
Tomáš Zdechovský — who has spoken out against Kremlin agents of influence operating inside the European Union — said he had never been to Russia, either before or after 2014. Michał Dworczyk — who condemns Russia’s invasion of Ukraine — gave the same answer. The Insider doubts those statements, even if in Dworczyk’s case, the border service records could be explained by another person having the same name and date of birth as the MEP.

articles.title: “Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
articles.body:
US Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the Russia sanctions law named after Lindsey Graham, has issued a sharp statement on the latest developments in Ukraine. He says that President Donald Trump and SpaceX chief Elon Musk should be held accountable for reported Starlink failures that could cripple Ukraine’s defense.
On 14 October, Ukraine’s military reported a Starlink disruption that halted its operations. It happened at the same time the country’s air defense stopped receiving intelligence on a Russian ballistic strike that killed three people in Kyiv. Both failures came right after the US struck a diesel deal with Russia, letting low volumes of fuel into global markets and America while pressure grew on Ukraine to stop hitting the Russian oil refineries that raise the cost of the war.
"Reports of Starlink failing in Ukraine are deeply alarming— potentially crippling air defense against Russia’s murderous missiles & drones. Trump & Musk must be held accountable," he says.
When the network falters, the war feels it
The alarm rests on how completely Ukraine leans on the system. SpaceX has reportedly throttled the StarShield military package Ukrainian drones use, with connections dropping once the drones move at speed, and breaking a series of missions.
Ukraine neither owns nor controls Starlink, and the latest limits revived long-running fears that its battlefield lifeline can be dialed down from outside the country.
Blumenthal’s demand sits inside a broader revolt in Congress. A bipartisan group of 12 senators wrote Trump on 13 October urging him to rescind his deal letting Russian diesel back to market, calling the Treasury’s General License No. 135 a gift to Moscow that should be withdrawn.
They pressed him instead to use the Graham-Leach-Bliley Act he signed in September to squeeze Russia and its enablers, above all, China.
"If there's one lesson from Trump's mindless warmongering, it's that we need to break our dependence on foreign imports of fossil fuels & embrace alternate sources of energy," he said.

articles.title: Russia Hits Kyiv Power Plant With Ballistic Missiles Two Days After Trump’s “Energy Ceasefire”
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Hits Kyiv Power Plant With Ballistic Missiles Two Days After Trump’s “Energy Ceasefire”
Russian forces struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles on October 13, hitting Combined Heat and Power Plant No. 4 (CHPP-4), one of the capital’s key sources of both electricity and heating, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said Ukraine again received no advance warning of the launch from its partners.
Emergency services are currently working to extinguish a fire at a damaged residential building following impacts across the capital.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Domestic defense detection systems identified the incoming missiles only as they approached the city.
Intelligence sources indicate that additional ballistic launches are being prepared by Russian forces. The strike hits key infrastructure despite Ukraine supporting a pause in targeting energy facilities during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Local authorities noted that continued strikes on energy facilities without advance partner warnings create ongoing danger for civilians. Efforts remain focused on supplying air defense units with necessary interceptors to respond to threats.
The previous night, Russian forces launched over 100 aerial weapons, including drones and five ballistic missiles that struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv and destroyed a residential building in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring 41 others.
Zelenskyy stated that Ukraine received no early warning from its international partners regarding that ballistic launch either, emphasizing that advance intelligence is critical to saving civilian lives given the extremely short flight time.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Sybiha: Putin must face consequences for rejecting peace, not incentives to continue war
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha called on international partners to increase pressure on Russia through sanctions and provide Ukraine with additional air defense systems, stressing that Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin must be held accountable for rejecting peace.
“Putin has delivered yet another negative “response” to the proposal of an energy ceasefire announced by President Trump and supported by President Zelenskyy. Instead of one “yes” to peace efforts — 39 missiles and more than 120 drones,” Sybiha said on X on Wednesday, commenting on Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities.
He said energy infrastructure facilities were the main targets of the strikes. At least three people were killed in Kyiv and more than 20 others were injured. Kyiv and Kharkiv came under massive attacks, while rescue and repair crews across Ukraine were dealing with the aftermath.
Sybiha said Russia was not only attacking Ukraine but was also openly challenging the United States and showing contempt for every effort to stop the war.
“There can be no economic rewards for aggression. No sanctions relief. No concessions that allow Russia to finance its next wave of terror,” Sybiha said.
He said every dollar flowing into Russia’s war budget becomes an additional resource for attacks on Ukrainian civilians and poses a threat to transatlantic security.
Sybiha called on partners to respond to the Russian attacks by tightening sanctions, strengthening enforcement and immediately providing Ukraine with additional air defense systems.
“Putin must face consequences for rejecting peace, not receive incentives to continue the war,” the minister said.

articles.title: Russian missile hits Kiev power plant as Zelenskyy flags lack of Western warning
articles.body:
A Russian ballistic missile has struck a power plant in Kiev without Ukraine receiving advance warning from its Western allies, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine relies heavily on Western, particularly US, intelligence to detect incoming Russian attacks and help identify targets of its own.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kiev. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Facebook.
"The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically the CHP-4. Unfortunately, it was hit."
AFP journalists in the Ukrainian capital reported hearing several blasts.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine's systems detected the missiles only as they neared the city.
"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.
At least two people were killed in the same attack, which also struck a residential building in the Desnianskyi district, said Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Around 20 others were wounded, he said.
"Energy ceasefire"
Overnight from Monday to Tuesday, Kiev residents heard explosions from Russian strikes before air raid sirens sounded, something that has occurred only rarely in the past.
On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials attributed the situation to the Russian military's use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack killed one person and damaged houses in the town of Balakovo on the Volga River in Russia's Saratov region, Governor Roman Busargin said on Telegram, without providing further details.
Balakovo is home to a nuclear power plant and a hydropower station, whose dam spans the Volga River.
On Sunday, US President Trump made a surprise "energy ceasefire" announcement on his Truth Social network, saying Russia and Ukraine had agreed to end their punishing long-range strikes on power plants and oil refineries.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy for strikes on Russian oil refineries and on Saturday suggested it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".

articles.title: Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities
articles.body:
Ukraine is drafting crisis scenarios for November to March as Russian strikes target the country’s biggest cities, Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov said on 13 October after chairing a meeting with donor-country diplomats and humanitarian organizations. His deputy Iryna Vereshchuk warned the same day that this winter may bring a new type of humanitarian crisis. She asked donors to be ready with fast extra funding.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s grid deep into winter before: last February, it launched more than 500 missiles and drones as temperatures fell below −20°C. Strikes have continued despite a US-announced energy truce Moscow has not confirmed. Kyiv now wants donors ready to pay for the humanitarian fallout in advance.
Crisis scenarios for November to March
The core task is clear crisis scenarios and synchronized response plans for that period, Budanov wrote. The government is building a baseline threat scenario through the State Emergency Service, while the military and intelligence will provide a risk assessment.
“The available resource must be concentrated where people will have the hardest time,” Budanov wrote.
Ukraine, he added, must hold its rear as reliably as the Defense Forces hold the front line.
What officials mean by a new type of crisis
A war of rear areas is underway, Vereshchuk wrote. Russia is changing tactics in an attempt to deepen the humanitarian crisis, especially in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Dnipro, she added.
Vereshchuk did not define what makes the crisis new, but she tied her warning to the big cities.
“This winter, it is the big cities that may become the testing ground of our national resilience,” she wrote.
Humanitarian organizations must adapt their plans to protect and support civilians, Vereshchuk wrote. Donors, she said, must be ready to provide additional crisis-response funding quickly.
The capital lags behind
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on 13 October that even border and frontline oblasts were ahead of Kyiv on resilience plans as of mid-October. Even single hits by Shahed attack drones can cut power and water across much of the capital, he noted. He also began consultations on urgent security and management steps to fix the situation in the city.
Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid
Russia carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission in the week to 11 October, Zelenskyy said. Overnight on 14 October, Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and critical infrastructure. The barrage left at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said.
